text: Now concerning the matters you wrote about: it is good for a man not to touch a woman.
But because of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.
The husband should give his wife what he owes her, and likewise the wife her husband.
The wife does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by mutual agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
I say this as a concession, not as a command.
I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God—one has this gift, another has that.

versions.text: I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind, another of another.
versions.explanation: "One of one kind, another of another" is stilted and hard to follow when read aloud; the suggested wording keeps the sense of ὁ μὲν οὕτως, ὁ δὲ οὕτως while flowing naturally in speech.

text: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain as I am.
But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. It is better to marry than to burn with passion.
To the married I give this charge—not I, but the Lord: a wife must not separate from her husband
(but if she does separate, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and a husband must not divorce his wife.
To the rest I say—I, not the Lord: if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her.
And if any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him.
For the unbelieving husband is made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.

versions.text: For the unbelieving husband is made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy through the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
versions.explanation: "Through the brother" is opaque for a hearer, since "the brother" has no antecedent in the sentence. The Greek ἀδελφῷ here refers to the believing husband; making that explicit preserves the parallel with the first clause and reads clearly aloud.

text: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not bound. God has called us to peace.
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
Only let each person live the life the Lord has assigned to him, the life to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches.
Was anyone already circumcised when he was called? He should not undo it. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? He should not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; what counts is keeping God's commandments.
Each should remain in the condition in which he was called.
Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it trouble you. But if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.
For the slave who was called in the Lord is the Lord's freedman; likewise the free man who was called is Christ's slave.
You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.
Brothers, each one should remain with God in the condition in which he was called.

versions.text: Brothers, each of us should remain with God in the condition in which he was called.
versions.explanation: The Greek is a third-person imperative addressed to the readers (ἕκαστος ... μενέτω), not a first-person plural. "Each of us" shifts the person and also clashes grammatically with the following "he was called."

text: Now concerning virgins: I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.

versions.text: Now concerning the unmarried: I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.
versions.explanation: παρθένων specifically means "virgins" (those never married), a narrower group than "the unmarried," which in verse 8 renders ἀγάμοις (which includes the formerly married). Keeping the distinction preserves the flow of the argument through verses 28, 34, 36-38.

text: I think, then, that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free of a wife? Do not seek a wife.
But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will face troubles in this life, and I would spare you that.
This is what I mean, brothers: the time is short. From now on, those who have wives should live as though they had none,
those who mourn as though they did not mourn, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, those who buy as though they owned nothing,
and those who use the world as though they were not engrossed in it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is concerned about the Lord's affairs, how to please the Lord.
But the married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how to please his wife,

and his interests are divided. The unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the Lord's affairs, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how to please her husband.
I say this for your own benefit, not to put any restraint on you, but to promote good order and undivided devotion to the Lord.
If anyone thinks he is acting improperly toward the virgin he is engaged to, and if his passions are strong and it has to be, let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning—they should marry.
But whoever stands firm in his heart, being under no compulsion but having control over his own will, and has made up his mind to keep his betrothed as she is, he will do well.

versions.text: But whoever stands firm in his heart, being under no compulsion but having control over his own will, and has made up his mind to keep her as she is, he will do well.
versions.explanation: The pronoun "her" has no antecedent in this verse, which is confusing when the passage is heard rather than read; naming the betrothed (as in verse 36 and 38) makes the sentence self-contained.

text: So then, the one who marries his betrothed does well, and the one who does not marry her will do better.
A wife is bound as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, only in the Lord.
Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is—and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
